_what_this_is: The standing rule that a Tier A change is reviewed by a session OTHER than the one that wrote it, made mechanical. Until 2026-09-15 it lived only in prose and in ad-hoc open-work-row warnings ('the session which wrote the code shares its own blind spot'), which is a rule enforced by remembering. Push-gate check 13 (tools/tier_a_review_gate.py) reads this file.
_how_it_works: A push that changes code serving a Tier A resource must leave an OPEN obligation here naming this session and those resources. The gate DENIES a push that touches Tier A code with no covering obligation, and DENIES any record whose reviewer is its own author. Recording the obligation is the author's job and takes one entry; discharging it is somebody else's and cannot be faked by the author.
_what_it_does_NOT_claim: That a review happened, or that it was any good. It is a record that the obligation EXISTS and was not self-signed. A gate cannot read a review; it can only refuse to let one be skipped silently or signed by its own author.
_scope: Tier A resources, derived from docs/CRITICALITY-TIERS.md. Never a second hand-kept copy of that list -- if the register cannot be parsed the gate FAILS CLOSED and says so.

merge_policy.note: Read by tools/sairn_rebase_resolve.py, from the COMMON ANCESTOR of a conflict, never from the conflicted file. This ledger is append-only across four clones, so a rebase conflict here is almost always "both sides added records" -- which has a correct answer, unlike a source file. The tool 3-way merges by the identity below, REFUSES on a deleted record or on one both sides changed differently, and stages nothing unless the validator passes.

records.verdict: REVIEWED. The IOLTA module stands and is the best-reasoned money code I have read here; TWO REAL FINDINGS, neither fixed by me -- I hold a review claim, not the files. (1) allocation_vs_ledger CANNOT disagree, confirmed across eight shapes -- plain, unreadable amount, absent client_id, non-string client_id, whitespace id, voided row, a null row, and a 500-row float mix -- agrees:true every time. NOT A FINDING: the file already says exactly this, marks it structural:true, excludes it from legs_compared and spells out the non-independence in its own field. I verified rather than accepted it, which is the only thing a reviewer can add to a claim that is already self-reported. (2) The on-or-before boundary is CORRECT: a transaction dated ON the statement date lands in ledger_as_of, the day after lands in movement_after_statement. (3) FINDING ONE, AND IT IS THE ONE YOU SUSPECTED, WORSE THAN PARTIAL. Undated rows are excluded from BOTH sides of the date split, so asOfCents + afterStatementCents silently stops equalling ledgerCents. Driven: one dated 100 dollar deposit plus one UNDATED 500 dollar deposit, with clientTotalCents supplied so two legs compare, returns status AGREES, legs_disagreeing [], device_vs_server true, bank_vs_ledger true -- while 50000 cents of client trust money is reconciled by nothing. The only cue is undated_rows:1 nested inside a leg that says agrees:true. The CONTROL is what makes it a defect rather than a limit: the same 500 dollars DATED after the statement also returns AGREES, but there it is honest, because movement_after_statement_cents reports 50000 and a reader can see where the money went. Post-statement money is ACCOUNTED; undated money is DROPPED, and the two are presented identically. This is the file's own no-single-matches-boolean principle -- a green verdict from a comparison never made -- reappearing one axis over. SUGGESTED FIX USES THE MODULE'S OWN EXISTING PATTERN AND CHANGES NO ARITHMETIC: a money-conservation identity beside row_conservation asserting asOf + after === ledger over readable non-voided rows, with bank_vs_ledger.agrees unable to be true while it fails. (4) FINDING TWO, A SCOPE LIMIT THAT IS NOT DISCLOSED: OUTSTANDING ITEMS. YOUR SECOND CHALLENGE -- AN alfEnterApp THAT PASSES THE REGEX AND STILL DOES NOT PURGE. FIVE, AND THE FIRST IS THE ONE THAT MATTERS. Each driven through your own fn()/balancedFrom() and both regexes:

records.verdict:
REVIEWED BY ATTACKING IT. Probe green here, 11/11 arms, all 7 mutations refused, worktree byte-identical after. You asked for three specific attempts; all three are answered, one of them found what you asked for and one of them found something you did not ask about.

(1) YES, THERE IS ANOTHER EQUIVALENT MUTANT, AND YOUR OWN FILE DOCUMENTS IT. Dropping the MANAGEMENT_ROLES term from seesAllRows -- `return !!(BROAD_READ_ROLES[session.role])` -- is EQUIVALENT for every role. Driven across owner, admin, estimator, roofer, foreman, office, undefined, '' and 'constructor': identical to the original every time. Dropping the BROAD_READ term, which is your mutation 6, is NOT equivalent (estimator diverges), so the pair is asymmetric and only one half is killable. The reason is the paragraph you wrote at api/rf-auth.js:547 -- MANAGEMENT_ROLES is a SUBSET of BROAD_READ_ROLES, so `!BROAD` alone gives the same answer at all 21 sites. NOT A DEFECT IN THE CODE: keeping both terms is the right call and your comment argues it correctly. It IS a bound on what the probe establishes. Mutations 5 and 6 read as "the role set is under control" and what they actually establish is control over one of the two terms; the other cannot be killed by any mutation until a management role exists that is not a broad reader. Your withdrawn-mutant note is the right place to say so, because the next person to read that note will take it as the complete list of equivalences you looked for.

(2) NO, AND THAT IS THE RIGHT ANSWER. I could not write a seesAllRows that passes your null arm and still admits a sessionless caller. Driven on null, undefined, 0, '', false and {}: `!session` catches the first five, and {} gives MANAGEMENT_ROLES[undefined] || BROAD_READ_ROLES[undefined], which is false. The arm is sound and the predicate is sound at that boundary.

BUT THE ROLE LOOKUP ITSELF ADMITS EIGHT STRINGS IT SHOULD NOT, AND THIS IS THE FINDING. MANAGEMENT_ROLES and BROAD_READ_ROLES are plain object literals, so `M[session.role]` walks the prototype chain. Driven against the REAL module, not a copy: seesAllRows({role:'constructor'}) is TRUE, and ownsRow({role:'constructor', employee_id:'E9'}, {assigned_employee_id:'SOMEBODY_ELSE'}) is TRUE. Same for '__proto__', 'toString', 'valueOf', 'hasOwnProperty', 'isPrototypeOf', 'propertyIsEnumerable' and 'toLocaleString'. Eight role strings grant full cross-assignee read and write on rf_claims and rf_claim_photos, both Tier A.

NOT REACHABLE TODAY, AND WHY THAT IS STILL WORTH FIXING. Provisioning refuses it at api/rf-auth.js:310 with `RF_ROLES.indexOf(role) === -1` -- an Array indexOf, which has no prototype chain, so the allowlist genuinely closes it. So the predicate is correct because of a check 250 lines away in a different branch, not because of its own arithmetic. That is the eighth cross-domain discipline's shape exactly: a guard that holds for a reason nothing local states. Object.create(null), a Set, or Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call would make it correct on its own terms. And it bears directly on this probe: a mutation that removed the RF_ROLES check at :310 would be killed by nothing in these seven arms, which is the one place these two files are coupled and neither says so.

(3) NO, AND THE REASON IS ONE ARGUMENT ORDER IN ONE Object.assign. Every gate call site I could find reads the COLUMN: the rf_claims write branch (:5798), the claim-photo read (:5855) and write (:5877), and assess_damage (:7059) each run their own server-side select for assigned_employee_id and hand that row to ownsRow, which reads row.assigned_employee_id. ownsRow never sees the caller payload, as you say.

WHAT IS ATTACKER-INFLUENCED IS THE data BLOB, AND IT IS ONE LINE FROM MATTERING. The write branch stores `Object.assign({}, payload, norm.money)` and deletes exactly two keys from it -- money_summary and id. It does NOT delete assigned_employee_id. So a narrow-role roofer writing a claim already assigned to them CAN put any employee id into data.assigned_employee_id; the column keeps the correct value, which is the part you got right. The only thing that makes the poisoned copy inert is the ORDER in the read branch at :5778: `Object.assign({}, x.data || {}, { ..., assigned_employee_id: x.assigned_employee_id || null, ... })` puts the column LAST, so it overwrites the blob. Swap those two arguments, or add a second read path that spreads data last, and the stored row becomes attacker-influenced on precisely the field the gate is named for. Nothing in the suite asserts that overlay order. The permanent fix is one more line in the write branch's delete list, beside money_summary, rather than a dependency on argument order in another branch.

AND ONE ARM WHOSE LABEL DOES NOT DESCRIBE WHAT IT DEMONSTRATES. Mutation 3 is titled "an auth failure becomes an authorisation pass". Driven: it does not. With ownsRow's own guard removed, seesAllRows still refuses a null session, so control reaches `row && row.assigned_employee_id === session.employee_id` and throws TypeError: Cannot read properties of null. The mutant IS killed and the runtime failure is fail-closed, so the arm is doing real work -- but it kills on a crash, not on a refusal, and with row=null it returns false rather than true. The label is what a future reader will trust when deciding whether the null-session path is covered by a REFUSAL, and on that question this arm says less than it appears to.

VERDICT: the probe is good and mutation 4's provenance note -- withdrawing an equivalent mutant and replacing it with one that reaches the direct call site, rather than deleting it -- is the best thing in the file. Three things to act on: the MANAGEMENT_ROLES term is unkillable and the note should say so; the role lookup should not resolve inherited properties, on a Tier A gate, however well the allowlist currently covers it; and assigned_employee_id belongs in the write branch's delete list so the read branch's argument order stops being load-bearing. None is a reason to hold the commit.

records.verdict:
REVIEWED BY DRIVING IT. Control green here, 12/12; the guarded suite 47/47 clean. You named three things to check and not the diff. All three are answered, two of them found something, and one of the two is a real coverage gap rather than a note.

(1) NO -- ALL FOUR expect REGEXES ARE VACUOUS, AND I MEASURED IT RATHER THAN ARGUING IT. The suite prints every PASSING arm as `  ok   NO PO NUMBER: the bill is HELD`, so the label you match on is in the output of a run where that arm PASSED. Driven on a CLEAN, all-47-passing run: NO PO NUMBER, BILLED MORE THAN THE PO, PARTIAL DELIVERY and DIFFERENT VENDOR each appear exactly once, on an `ok` line.

THE DECISIVE EXPERIMENT. I planted a mutation with nothing to do with any of the four refusals -- sbPONext() returns the constant 'PO-2026-001', which breaks the PO-sequence arms in section 5 -- and re-ran. The suite goes RED (exit 1, correct), and 4 OF 4 expect regexes still match. So the second arm of every mutation, `and it fails on the X arm`, would have credited the suite for catching a defect it did not catch. The exit-code arm is real; the expect arm is decoration on any failure landing after section 2.

WHY IT IS DIRECTIONAL, WHICH MATTERS FOR HOW BAD IT IS. `ok()` is `assert.ok(cond,label)`, so the suite ABORTS at the first failure. A mutation caught inside section 2 aborts before the later labels print, and the expect regex is then accidentally right. A failure anywhere AFTER section 2 -- sections 5, 7 and 8, which is roughly 30 of the 47 assertions -- leaves all four labels printed as passes. So the arm is correct only when the mutation lands early, and every one of your four does. It is not wrong today; it cannot detect being wrong tomorrow.

THE FIX IS ONE LINE EACH AND I TESTED IT ON THE SAME OUTPUTS. `expect: /AssertionError[^\n]*NO PO NUMBER/i`. On the real no-PO mutation the strict form MATCHES for that arm and does NOT match for BILLED MORE THAN THE PO, so it identifies WHICH arm caught it; on the unrelated PO-sequence mutation it matches none of the four. Both directions driven.

(2) THE FIFTH REFUSAL IS DRIVABLE, AND BY THE TECHNIQUE YOUR OWN MUTATION 1 ALREADY USES. You could not disable `if(!pos.length) return {ok:false,...}` without pos[0] throwing -- because removing the guard is not the only surgical option. Making it return EARLY with a pass never reaches pos[0]:

    if(!pos.length) return {ok:true,reasons:[]};

which is the identical shape to your mutation 1 on `if(!po_num)`. Driven: exit 1, no TypeError, and the suite refuses it on the arm that is actually about it -- `A PO NUMBER THAT EXISTS NOWHERE: held`. So the branch should be added, and the note explaining why it was left out should go rather than be corrected: the reasoning was about deleting the guard, and the paragraph reads as a property of the function.

(3) FOUR IS NOT THE RIGHT STOPPING POINT. sbMatchPure has more refusals than the five you counted, and I drove the three you did not:

  duplicate-PO ambiguity  `if(pos.length>1)`               -> suite CATCHES it
  nothing received        `if(!recs.length)`               -> suite CATCHES it
  a RECEIPT naming a different vendor than the PO          -> SUITE DOES NOT CATCH IT

THAT LAST ONE IS THE FINDING. Disabling

    if(sbVendorKey(r.vendor)&&sbVendorKey(r.vendor)!==sbVendorKey(po.vendor))

leaves the suite GREEN -- exit 0, no assertion fired. And it is live product behaviour on a user-entered field, not dead code: the receiving form has a Vendor input (`rcvvendor`, sairnbiz.html:859) and sb_recv rows store `vendor: $('rcvvendor').value.trim()` (:2890). The suite mentions receipt-vendor nowhere at all -- grep for "a receipt names" returns 0, and for any receipt/vendor pairing returns nothing.

WHY IT IS THE ONE THAT MATTERS ON THIS GATE. The PO-vendor check you did mutate separates a clerical error from a redirected payment. The RECEIPT-vendor check is the one that notices goods arriving from a party the purchase order did not authorise -- the third document disagreeing with the first about WHO, rather than about how much. On a three-way match that is not a lesser case of the same thing. So there is an untested refusal inside a tested function, which is the exact condition your own header says a control exists to surface; the control surfaced the branch you wrote down and missed the branch you did not.

Also worth noting for whoever adds them: the `!pos.length` refusal carries THREE distinct messages (never existed / one voided / all voided) and `!recs.length` carries two, and the difference between them is the difference between sending somebody to the loading dock and sending them to a receipt they corrected -- your own comment says so. Those are message-level, not gate-level, so they belong in the suite rather than in this control.

VERDICT: the control is well built and the three-way plant guard -- uniqueness, difference, materialisation, with COULD NOT PLANT as exit 2 rather than a pass -- is the part other controls on this platform should copy. Section 5 is the right arm and it holds. Two things to act on: the expect regexes need the AssertionError anchor or they are not testing what they say, and the receipt-vendor refusal is uncontrolled AND untested on a Tier A gate. The fifth-branch note should be replaced by the branch. None of it is a reason to hold the commit.

records.verdict: REVIEWED by fourth. All three targets check out, and the first one only checks out because of a file hank did not name. (1) FAIL-CLOSED ON A WRITE PATH IS THE RIGHT CALL, and the reasoning stands on its own: a gate that opens during an outage lets the outage perform the exact thing the gate exists to prevent, which is not true of a read. BUT IT ONLY WORKS IF THE DEPENDENCY RAISES, and the catch is worthless if validateLicenseKey swallows its own failures and returns valid:false -- that would answer 403 'That licence is not valid' when the truth is 'nobody could check', which is COULD-NOT-TELL folded into a verdict (PR 1.11) in an auth decision. READ RATHER THAN TRUSTED: api/_lib/license.js throws on all three could-not-tell states -- missing SUPABASE config (code CONFIG), a fetch that rejects (UPSTREAM), and any non-2xx from the licence store (UPSTREAM) -- and returns valid:false ONLY for a key the table does not contain. So the 503 LICENCE_UNCHECKED and 403 BAD_LICENCE really are different answers to different questions. Confirmed. (2) NOTHING DOWNSTREAM READS THE BODY'S shopId. Traced both ends: the only producer is stonedesk.html:19691, which sends it with a comment saying the server ignores it and it is kept so an older deployment survives the window; and bridge.js:22 records that bridge_data is written and never read at all, so there is no consumer to break. Accept-and-ignore is the right shape for a deploy window and the two halves ship together. (3) THE ORPHANED ROWS ARE THE RESIDUAL AND THEY ARE WORSE THAN ORPHANED. Deferring the delete was right -- it is a database action and no clone has that access -- but the record should say what is actually sitting there rather than 'orphaned': every pre-existing bridge_data row has a CUSTOMER'S RAW LICENCE KEY as its primary key. That is a bearer secret in a table, which is the same class the NHI register names for tenant_key ('NEVER the raw licence key -- that is a bearer secret and must not sit in a log table'), and it does not stop being one because nothing reads it. RECOMMEND it be raised as a named Michael action with the exposure stated, not left inside a review note: the rows are unreachable by the product and fully readable by anyone with database access, and they will outlive everyone's memory of why they are there. api/bridge-push-auth.test.js green.
